title: Performing Arts: Music, Dance and Drama
summary: Art is the aesthetic expression of the characteristics of the human mind – emotions called 'ras' (the ultimate satisfaction of aanand). Nine rasas (navras): Hasya (laughter), Bhayanak (fear), Rudra (anger), Karun (pathos), Veer (courage), Adbhut (wonder), Vibhatsa (disgust), Shaanti (peace), Shringaar (love/decoration). Sketching, painting and sculpture are visual arts; singing, dancing and acting are performing arts. Performing arts educated the masses, spread religion and social reform and are now also entertainment. Festivals like Lohri are celebrated with Bhangra and Giddha; many songs and dances began with fertility rites. Notes of music: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni.

The earliest tradition of music goes back to the Sama Veda, whose slokas were set to music and chanted with prescribed pitch and accent; the earliest text on performing arts is Bharata's Natyashastra (between 2nd century BC and 2nd century AD) with six chapters on music; Matanga's Brihaddeshi (8th–9th century AD) first named and discussed ragas; Sarangadeva's Sangita Ratnakara (13th century) mentions 264 ragas; ancient texts mention flute, drums, veena and cymbals; Samudragupta, King Bhoja and Someshvara patronised music and Samudragupta is shown playing the veena on coins; Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century) has songs set in ragas on the love of Radha and Krishna; Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabharati; the Saivite Nayanars and Vaishnavite Alvars set psalms to music. In the medieval period Sufis (qawwali in khanqahs) and Bhakti saints (kirtan, bhajan – Kabir, Mirabai, Surdas, Chandidas, Tulsidas, Vidyapati) encouraged music; Amir Khusrau, Baz Bahadur and Rupmati (new ragas), Ibrahim Adil Shah II (Kitab-i-Nauras), Tansen and Baiju Bawra of Akbar's court; Babur, Humayun, Akbar and Swami Haridas; Pundarika Vittal wrote Ragamala.
## Hindustani, Carnatic, modern and folk music

Classical music has two traditions: Hindustani (North; traced to the Delhi Sultanate and Amir Khusrau; descendants of Tansen; styles Dhrupad, Dhamar, Thumri, Khayal, Tappa; ragas Bahar, Bhairavi, Darbari, Yaman, Megh Malhar, etc.; instruments sitar, sarod, santoor, sarangi, pakhawaj, tabla, flute, shehnai; gharanas – hereditary linkage of musicians in the guru-shishya parampara: Gwalior, Kirana, Jaipur) and Carnatic (South; composers Shyama Shastri, Thyagaraja and Mutthuswami Dikshitar between 1700 and 1850, Purandaradasa; main compositions are kritis, devotional; accompanied by flute, veena, nadaswaram, mridangam, ghatam; Carnatic alapana is similar to alap and tillana to tarana; both stress tala). With British rule violin and clarinet were adopted and orchestration, cassettes and music institutions replaced the master–disciple system. Folk music represents the emotion of the masses and marks every event: Mand (Rajasthan), Bhatiali (Bengal), Ragini (Haryana), Gulraj (Kashmir), Pandvani (MP), Sojkhwani during Muharram, carols.

The Rig Veda mentions dance; the bronze Dancing Girl of Harappa shows dance in the Indus culture; Shiva as Nataraja symbolises the creation and destruction of the cosmic cycle; temples show dancers. Classical dances: Kathakali, Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Manipuri, Kuchipudi, Odissi (also Mohiniattam). Temple dance had a religious object and court dance was entertainment. Bharatanatyam and Mohiniattam developed in temples of the south; Yakshagana (a form of Kathakali in Kerala) tells stories of the Ramayana and Mahabharata; Kathak and Manipuri are mostly related to Krishna and his leela; Odissi is related to the worship of Lord Jagannath; Kathak moved to the courts and was promoted by Muslim rulers (not Aurangzeb); Wajid Ali Shah began the Lucknow gharana (Birju Maharaj). Folk dances: Bihu (Assam), Garba (Gujarat), Bhangra and Giddha (Punjab), Bamboo dance (Mizoram), Koli (Maharashtra fishermen), Dhumal (Kashmir), Chhau (Bengal); martial dances: Cholia (Uttarakhand), Kalaripayattu (Kerala), Thang-ta (Manipur). Bharata's Natyashastra divides dance into nritta (pure footwork, pada sanchalan), nritya (anga sanchalan, expression) and natya (abhinaya, drama).

Drama's origin is traced to the Vedas; the Ramayana mentions women's drama troupes and Kautilya's Arthashastra mentions musicians, dancers and shows; drama could begin with a child's mimicry. Bharata wrote the Natyashastra and the plays Asura Parajaya and Amrit Manthan; for him drama was the perfect means of communication, with nat and nati, music, dance, instruments, dialogue, themes and stage and an enclosed theatre; the shailoosh were professional drama companies and kushilavas professional singers of heroic tales. Bhasa wrote 13 plays (Swapnavasavadatta); Patanjali's Mahabhashya mentions Kamsavadha and Balibandha. In Buddha's and Mahavira's age drama spread religion. Sanskrit was used, with women and low-class characters speaking Prakrit; Kalidasa's Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Malavikagnimitra, Vikramorvashiyam; Bana Bhatta's Harshacharita; Vidyapati introduced Hindi and regional songs. Folk theatre in local dialect: Jatra and Kirtania Natak (Bengal), Bidesia (Bihar), Raas, Jhumar, Dhola Maru (Rajasthan), Raas, Nautanki, Swang, Bhand (UP), Bhavai (Gujarat), Lalit and Tamasha (Maharashtra), Kathakali and Yakshagana (South); props dhol, kartal, manjira, khanjira. Wajid Ali Shah patronised drama. Modern theatre began when a Russian, Gerasim Lebedev, founded a Bengali theatre in Calcutta; Shakespeare influenced Indian drama; stages got rolling curtains; a Parsi company in Bombay made it commercial; Shambhu Mitra, Feisal Alkazi, Badal Sarkar, Vijay Tendulkar experimented. Types now: stage, radio, Nukkar (street plays), mono-drama, musical theatre, skits, one-act plays. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda influenced dance, drama and painting all over India. Writers: Kalidasa (Meghadutam, Abhijnana Shakuntalam), Bharatendu (Neel Devi, Satya Harishchandra, Andher Nagri), Jaishankar Prasad (Chandragupta, Ajatashatru, Skandagupta etc.).

Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, Prayag Sangeet Samiti, Indira Kala Sangeet Vishwavidyalaya (Khairagarh), Kathak Kendra, National School of Drama, Bharatiya Kala Kendra, SPIC MACAY and Sangeet Natak Akademi promote the arts; Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan and Alla Rakha run institutions abroad; ICCR and the Ministry of Human Resource Development give grants, scholarships and fellowships and arrange exchanges. The arts elevate the soul, give balance and peace of mind, self-restraint, love for all and self-confidence, helping the development of personality.

vsa: Why is folk music an important part of our heritage? Give any two reasons.

It represents the emotion of the masses and marks every event of life – festivals, seasons, marriage and birth; it describes historical events and rituals and preserves local culture (Mand, Bhatiali, Ragini).
Name the two divisions of Indian classical music and one difference.

Hindustani music of North India and Carnatic music of South India; Hindustani styles include dhrupad, khayal and thumri with gharanas, while Carnatic music is based on devotional kritis of Thyagaraja and others.
What was the contribution of Baz Bahadur and Rupmati to music?
The legendary ruler of Malwa and his wife introduced new ragas.
State two similarities between Hindustani and Carnatic music.
Carnatic alapana is like Hindustani alap, tillana is like tarana, and both lay stress on tala.
What are the three broad categories of dance in the Natyashastra?
Nritta (pada sanchalan, pure movement), nritya (anga sanchalan, expression) and natya (abhinaya, dramatic acting).
What was the role of kushilavas and shailoosh in ancient drama?
Shailoosh were communities with professional drama companies; kushilavas were professional singers who dramatically sang heroic tales.
Name any four types of drama flourishing today.
Stage theatre, radio theatre, Nukkar (street plays), mono-drama, musical theatre, short skits and one-act plays (any four).
sa: Explain briefly the significance of performing arts.

Music, dance and drama express the nine rasas of human emotion, educated the masses from the Vedic age to the medieval period, spread religion and reform, and are now means of entertainment. They elevate the soul, bring peace of mind, self-restraint, love and self-confidence and so help in the development of personality.
Explain three facts about the earliest tradition of music in India.

It goes back to the Sama Veda, whose slokas were put to music and chanted with prescribed pitch and accent; Bharata's Natyashastra (2nd century BC–2nd century AD) is the earliest text on performing arts with six chapters on music; Matanga's Brihaddeshi first named ragas and Sangita Ratnakara lists 264 ragas.
Describe the Hindustani and Carnatic music traditions.

Hindustani music, traced to Amir Khusrau and Tansen, has styles like dhrupad, khayal and thumri and gharanas such as Gwalior and Kirana. Carnatic music, with the trinity Shyama Shastri, Thyagaraja and Dikshitar, has devotional kritis and is accompanied by veena, flute, mridangam and ghatam.
Write a note on the classical dances of India.

Kathakali, Bharatnatyam, Mohiniattam and Kuchipudi are southern dances; Kathak (Krishna leela, courts), Manipuri (Krishna) and Odissi (Jagannath) are northern and eastern. Temple dance had a religious object and court dance was for entertainment; Natyashastra divides dance into nritta, nritya and natya.
Explain the role of folk theatre in India.

Folk theatre used local dialect, was spontaneous and combined acting with music and dance; forms: Jatra, Nautanki, Tamasha, Bhavai, Raas, Yakshagana; instruments like dhol and manjira were props; they carried social messages and adapted classical forms.
la: Examine the role of Muslim rulers in the promotion of dance and music in India.

The Sultans and Mughals were great patrons. Amir Khusrau (1253–1325) introduced new ragas and encouraged musical performance; Sufis sang qawwali in khanqahs. Babur is said to have developed styles like qawwali and khayal; Humayun illustrated Indian music texts; Akbar composed songs and patronised Tansen, Baiju Bawra and Swami Haridas; Jahangir and Shah Jahan patronised musicians. Kathak was promoted in the courts of most Mughal rulers except Aurangzeb, and Wajid Ali Shah began the Lucknow gharana of dance. The largest number of Persian books on classical music were written even under Aurangzeb.
Examine the popularity of folk dances in India.

Folk dances evolved from the lives of common people and are performed in unison to express joys and sorrows, often linked to harvest and festivals: Bihu in Assam, Garba in Gujarat, Bhangra and Giddha in Punjab, Bamboo dance in Mizoram, Koli in Maharashtra, Dhumal in Kashmir, Chhau in Bengal, Mask dance in Ladakh, Wangla in Meghalaya, and martial dances like Cholia, Kalaripayattu and Thang-ta. They are part of every celebration and school programme and even of city culture.
Discuss the evolution and development of drama in ancient India.

Drama's origin is traced to the Vedas, and the Ramayana and Arthashastra mention drama and dancers. Bharata wrote the Natyashastra and the plays Asura Parajaya and Amrit Manthan, describing nat, nati, music, dance, instruments, dialogue and stage; the shailoosh and kushilavas were professionals. Bhasa wrote thirteen plays, Patanjali's Mahabhashya mentions Kamsavadha and Balibandha; Buddha and Mahavira used drama for preaching; Sanskrit plays by Kalidasa (Abhijnana Shakuntalam), Bana Bhatta and others had women and lower characters speaking Prakrit; folk theatre in local dialect developed alongside.
Describe the account of drama as per Bharata's Natyashastra.

Bharata's Natyashastra is the greatest text on drama and the performing arts. It describes nat (male) and nati (female) actors, music, dance, instruments, dialogues, themes and the stage, with an enclosed theatre; it says music and dance are essential parts of drama and calls drama a perfect means of communication. He wrote Asura Parajaya and Amrit Manthan and discusses the nine rasas and the classification of dance into nritta, nritya and natya.
